attribution_finding: Katz majority; Olmstead component is explicitly a paraphrase of the earlier majority.
fidelity_finding: Katz passage corresponds. Olmstead summary fairly conveys physical-intrusion/tangible-seizure basis for its holding.
pinpoint_finding: Katz 353 correct; Olmstead 464–466 better supports whole paraphrase than 466 alone.
scope_and_cutoff_finding: Katz rejects the controlling trespass doctrine in Olmstead/Goldman. Do not attribute Harlan's separate two-part expectation test to this majority quotation.
proposed_action_not_applied: No substantive attribution correction; optionally broaden Olmstead pinpoint to 464–466.
prior_repair_status: No repair performed in this audit

ledger_excerpt:
From Katz v. United States, 389 U.S. 347, 353 (1967):
"We conclude that the underpinnings of Olmstead and Goldman have been so eroded by our subsequent decisions that the 'trespass' doctrine there enunciated can no longer be regarded as controlling... The Government's activities in electronically listening to and recording the petitioner's words violated the privacy upon which he justifiably relied while using the telephone booth and thus constituted a 'search and seizure' within the meaning of the Fourth Amendment."

From Olmstead v. United States, 277 U.S. 438, 466 (1928):
The original majority holding that wiretapping telephone wires without physical trespass into the defendant's premises or seizure of tangible material did not violate the Fourth Amendment.
